# 1. Introduction
This analysis explores the relationships between monthly rent and property characteristics in Tokyo's 23 wards using descriptive statistics, visualizations, correlation analysis, and hypothesis testing.



# 2. Libraries
```{r libraries}
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
```



# 3. Data Overview
## 3.1 Load Data
```{r load-data}
# Load the preprocessed training dataset
df <- read.csv(
  "processed_train_data.csv",
  fileEncoding = "UTF-8-BOM"
)
```


## 3.2 Dataset Structure
```{r dataset-structure}
# Check dataset dimensions
cat("Number of observations:", nrow(df), "\n")
cat("Number of variables:", ncol(df), "\n")

# Examine variable names and data types
glimpse(df)
```



## 3.3 Missing Values
```{r missing-values}
# Calculate missing values for each variable
missing_summary <- df %>%
  summarise(
    across(
      everything(),
      list(
        missing_count = ~ sum(is.na(.x)),
        missing_rate = ~ mean(is.na(.x)) * 100
      )
    )
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = c("variable", ".value"),
    names_pattern = "^(.*)_(missing_count|missing_rate)$"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(missing_rate))


# Display missing values for all variables
missing_summary %>%
  mutate(missing_rate = round(missing_rate, 2)) %>%
  kable(
    col.names = c("Variable", "Missing Count", "Missing Rate (%)"),
    caption = "Missing Values by Variable"
  )
```



## 3.4 Descriptive Statistics
```{r descriptive-statistics} 
# Select key numerical variables with low missing rates
numeric_vars <- c(
  "rent",
  "area",
  "building_age",
  "floor",
  "total_floor",
  "walk_1"
)


# Summarize selected variables
summary(df[numeric_vars])
```



## 3.5 Rent Distribution
```{r rent-distribution, fig.width=9, fig.height=5} 
# Visualize the distribution of monthly rent
ggplot(df, aes(x = rent)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 60,
    fill = "steelblue",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = median(df$rent, na.rm = TRUE),
    color = "red",
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Monthly Rent",
    x = "Monthly Rent (JPY)",
    y = "Number of Properties"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)


# Zoom in on the main rental price range
ggplot(df, aes(x = rent)) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 10000,
    boundary = 0,
    fill = "steelblue",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = median(df$rent, na.rm = TRUE),
    color = "red",
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 500000)) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Monthly Rent (0-500,000 JPY)",
    x = "Monthly Rent (JPY)",
    y = "Number of Properties"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```


## 3.6 Log Transformation
```{r log_transformation}
# Examine the distribution of log-transformed rent
ggplot(df %>% filter(rent > 0), aes(x = log(rent))) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 50,
    fill = "steelblue",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Log-Transformed Monthly Rent",
    x = "Log(Monthly Rent)",
    y = "Number of Properties"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```



# 4. Relationships Between Rent and Numerical Variables
## 4.1 Scatter Plots
```{r numerical-scatter-plots, fig.width=10, fig.height=7}
# Select numerical variables for exploratory analysis
plot_vars <- c("area", "building_age", "walk_1")


# Reshape data for visualization
scatter_data <- df %>%
  select(rent, all_of(plot_vars)) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = all_of(plot_vars),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "value"
  )


# Plot relationships with monthly rent
ggplot(scatter_data, aes(x = value, y = rent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.12, size = 0.6, color = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(
    title = "Relationships Between Rent and Numerical Variables",
    x = "Property Characteristic",
    y = "Monthly Rent (JPY)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```



## 4.2 Correlation Analysis
```{r correlation-analysis}
# Select variables for correlation analysis
cor_vars <- c(
  "area",
  "building_age",
  "walk_1",
  "floor",
  "total_floor"
)


# Calculate Pearson and Spearman correlations with rent
correlation_results <- map_dfr(cor_vars, function(var) {

  complete_data <- df %>%
    select(rent, all_of(var)) %>%
    drop_na()

  tibble(
    variable = var,
    n = nrow(complete_data),
    pearson = cor(
      complete_data$rent,
      complete_data[[var]],
      method = "pearson"
    ),
    spearman = cor(
      complete_data$rent,
      complete_data[[var]],
      method = "spearman"
    )
  )
})


# Display correlation coefficients
correlation_results %>%
  mutate(across(c(pearson, spearman), ~ round(.x, 3))) %>%
  kable(
    caption = "Pearson and Spearman Correlations with Monthly Rent"
  )
```



# 5. Relationships Between Rent and Categorical Variables
## 5.1 Rental Prices by Ward
```{r ward-summary} 
# Calculate descriptive statistics by ward
ward_summary <- df %>%
  group_by(ward) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_rent = mean(rent, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_rent = median(rent, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_rent = sd(rent, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(median_rent))


# Display summary statistics
ward_summary %>%
  mutate(
    across(
      c(mean_rent, median_rent, sd_rent),
      ~ round(.x, 0)
    )
  ) %>%
  kable(
    caption = "Descriptive Statistics of Monthly Rent by Ward"
  )
```


## 5.2 Rent Distribution by Ward
```{r}
# Compare rent distributions across wards
ggplot(df, aes(x = reorder(ward, rent, median), y = rent)) +
  geom_boxplot(
    fill = "steelblue",
    color = "gray30",
    width = 0.65,
    outlier.alpha = 0.08,
    outlier.size = 0.5
  ) +
  coord_flip(ylim = c(0, 400000)) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::comma,
    breaks = seq(0, 400000, 50000)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Rent Distribution by Ward",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Monthly Rent (JPY)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 11),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()
  )

```


## 5.3 One-way ANOVA: Rent by ward
```{r one_way_anova_rent_by_ward}
# One-way ANOVA: Rent by ward
ward_anova <- aov(rent ~ ward, data = df)

summary(ward_anova)


# Eta-squared effect size
anova_table <- anova(ward_anova)

anova_table["ward", "Sum Sq"] / sum(anova_table[, "Sum Sq"])
```


## 5.4 Monthly Rent by Building Structure
```{r rent_by_building_structure}
df %>%
  group_by(building_structure) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_rent = mean(rent),
    median_rent = median(rent),
    sd_rent = sd(rent),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(median_rent)) %>%
  kable(
    caption = "Monthly Rent by Building Structure"
  )
```


## 5.5 Monthly Rent by Layout
```{r rent_by_layout}
# Compare monthly rent by layout
df %>%
  group_by(layout) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_rent = mean(rent),
    median_rent = median(rent),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(n)) %>%
  kable(
    caption = "Monthly Rent by Layout"
  )
```


## 5.6 Floor Area by Layout
```{r floor_area_by_layout}
# Compare floor area across common layouts
df %>%
  group_by(layout) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    median_area = median(area, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_area = mean(area, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(n >= 100) %>%
  arrange(median_area) %>%
  kable(
    caption = "Floor Area by Layout"
  )
```



# 6. Conclusion
Exploratory analysis revealed associations between rental prices and property characteristics, including floor area, building age, walking distance, and location.

These findings provide a foundation for feature selection and regression modeling in the subsequent analysis.
